KiteConfig keeps the basic facts about your app in one place. You write the name, the app id, the version and the build number once, and KiteConfig puts them where Android, iOS and the desktop expect to find them. Without it, each platform keeps its own copy, and sooner or later the copies stop matching.

Version 3.0.0 brought KiteConfig to the Kotlin Toolchain, the newer `./kotlin` command that builds a project from `project.yaml` and `module.yaml` files instead of Gradle. This update fixes two problems that showed up in the first real projects, so it is a good moment to try it.

## With the Kotlin Toolchain

Open a terminal in the folder that holds your `project.yaml` and run this command:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yuroyami/KiteConfig/main/toolchain/install-kiteconfig.sh | bash -s 3.0.1
```

The Kotlin Toolchain only loads plugins that live inside your project. So the script copies a small KiteConfig folder into `./kiteconfig`. If your `project.yaml` does not list that folder yet, the script prints the two lines to add. Commit the folder with the rest of your code. To update later, run the script again.

Then turn KiteConfig on in the `module.yaml` of your app:

```yaml
plugins:
  kiteconfig:
    enabled: true
    appName: Jetzy
    version: 4.1.1
    appId: com.example.jetzy
    locales: [ en, pt-BR ]
```

From there, your code gets a small generated `KiteBuildConfig` object that holds these values. `./kotlin do kiteSyncIos` writes the version, the build number, the app id and the languages into your Xcode project. `./kotlin check` tells you when the Xcode project has fallen behind, and it can also tell you when the Android settings in `module.yaml` disagree with KiteConfig. A version gives the same build number here as it does with the Gradle plugin. So a project can move from one to the other, and its store build numbers stay in order.

App icons, launch screens, `Info.plist` changes and desktop packaging still need the Gradle plugin. The [Kotlin Toolchain guide](https://github.com/yuroyami/KiteConfig/blob/main/toolchain/README.md) has the full setup.

## With Gradle

Add the plugin to the build file at the root of your project:

```kotlin
plugins {
    id("io.github.yuroyami.kiteconfig") version "3.0.1"
}
```

If you come from 2.x, one small thing changed in 3.0.0. When KiteConfig stops a build because a value is wrong, it now throws `KiteConfigException` instead of `GradleException`. The message is the same. This only matters if your own build code catches `GradleException` around KiteConfig. In that case, catch `RuntimeException` instead.

## What is new in 3.0.1

The KiteConfig folder in a Kotlin Toolchain project now asks for Kotlin 2.4.21, the same version that KiteConfig itself is built with. Before, the folder did not ask for any version. The Kotlin Toolchain then used its own older default, Kotlin 2.4.20, which could mean an extra download just for this folder.

Xcode projects with short item names now work. Xcode gives each item in a project a name of 24 letters and digits, but a project that someone wrote by hand often uses shorter names. KiteConfig refused to read such a project and stopped with an error. It now accepts every name that Xcode itself accepts. The Gradle plugin reads Xcode projects the same way, so it gets this fix too.

The install script is now part of the release, and the [Kotlin Toolchain guide](https://github.com/yuroyami/KiteConfig/blob/main/toolchain/README.md) explains what it does.

If you already use 3.0.0 with the Kotlin Toolchain, run the install script again with `3.0.1`. Gradle projects only need the new version number.

**Full changelog**: https://github.com/yuroyami/KiteConfig/compare/v3.0.0...v3.0.1
